verdicts.threatModel: The rule models an attacker or workload growing an unbounded Redis keyspace. Ember has no Redis client or server: Cargo.lock and pnpm-lock.yaml contain zero 'redis' entries, so no network cache exists for any attacker to fill.
verdicts.reachability: All 826 member locations (scanner raw file/line in execution.json legacy.data.internal-suite candidates; 526 in crates/raw, 111 crates/engine, 32 crates/tiff, rest in tests/UI) are generic `.set(` calls: TIFF IFD builder tag writes such as `ifd.set(t::COMPRESSION, Value::Short(..))`, JS Map/queue sets in test scripts, and in-memory test fixtures. None reach a Redis sink.
verdicts.impact: None. crates/tiff/src/writer.rs:34-36 shows IfdBuilder::set is `self.entries.insert(tag, value)` into an in-memory map used to build a DNG/TIFF file; there is no retention or expiration semantic to violate and no confidentiality, integrity or availability effect.
verdicts.rationale: Lexical match on `.set(` misclassified as a Redis write; the project has no Redis dependency and sampled sites (crates/engine/src/files.rs:2302, crates/raw/src/dngwrite.rs:140, crates/raw/src/vendor/pef.rs:560, crates/tiff/tests/roundtrip.rs:137, scripts/desktop/slider-command-queue.test.mjs:69) are TIFF tag builders or in-process maps. Devil's advocate: a hidden Redis use via a transitive crate would still appear in Cargo.lock, which has none.

verdicts.threatModel: SQL injection requires attacker-influenced text concatenated into a SQL statement executed by a database engine. Ember links no SQL client (no rusqlite/sqlx/diesel/libsqlite3 in Cargo.lock); its Lightroom import uses an in-repo read-only SQLite file parser (crates/engine/src/lightroom_catalog.rs:11 `lightroom_sqlite::{Database, LiveTable}`) that walks tables, not SQL text.
verdicts.reachability: All 23 members were inspected at their exact lines: 15 are React JSX/template literals building className or label strings (e.g. apps/lightcraft-desktop/web/src/library/Filmstrip.tsx:229, App.tsx:158 `${window.innerWidth}x${window.innerHeight}`), 4 are egui font registration and test asserts containing the words 'select'/'update'/'delete' (crates/ui-egui/src/theme.rs:280, crates/pipeline/src/masks.rs:695), 1 a command-registry doc string (crates/engine/src/cmd/denoise.rs:654), and 1 a regex error message (scripts/desktop/gate.mjs:33). No grep hit exists for a SELECT/INSERT INTO/UPDATE/DELETE FROM string literal in crates or apps sources.
verdicts.impact: None. No SQL statement is constructed or executed at any member location, so no query integrity or data confidentiality is at risk.
verdicts.rationale: Scanner keyed on SQL keywords ('select', 'update', 'delete', 'insert') appearing near string interpolation; every site is UI markup, font maps, or test assertion text. Devil's advocate: the Lightroom catalog path does read SQLite, but through a structural parser with no query text and none of the 23 members sit in it.

verdicts.threatModel: The rule models partial database writes across a crash or concurrent writer leaving persisted state inconsistent. No attacker capability is involved; the question is whether adjacent writes target a transactional store.
verdicts.reachability: The 71 members are adjacent `.insert(` calls on in-process HashMap/BTreeMap/serde_json::Map/HashSet values (e.g. crates/desktop-host/src/merge.rs:167 `self.current.insert(..)`, crates/engine/src/lightroom_catalog.rs:662 `geometry.insert("rect"..)`, crates/engine/src/cmd/library.rs:650 `params.insert(k, v)`, apps/lightcraft-cli/src/main.rs:464). The catalog sites (crates/catalog/src/lib.rs:759, keywords.rs:552) mutate in-memory indexes whose persistence goes through the catalog's own append log, not these inserts.
verdicts.impact: None. In-memory map mutations within one function are not durable writes; a crash discards them wholesale, so no torn persisted state or data loss arises from the lack of a transaction boundary at these lines.
verdicts.rationale: Lexical match on multiple `.insert(` calls; none is a database write. Devil's advocate: catalog durability is real, but it is enforced at the log append layer (crates/catalog has dedicated torn-append tests, crates/catalog/src/tests_torn_append.rs), not at these map inserts, so this rule cannot find a defect here.

verdicts.threatModel: A network or raw.pixls.us-side attacker substituting the bytes served at xtask/src/main.rs:333 (https://raw.pixls.us/getfile.php/2414/nice/Sony%20-%20ILCE-7M3%20-%2014bit%2014bit%20compressed%20%283:2%29.ARW) for corpus file arw-sony-a7m3-compressed.arw, aiming to feed a malicious raw into Ember's decoder tests.
verdicts.reachability: xtask/src/main.rs:333 is the URL field of the RAW_SAMPLES tuple for arw-sony-a7m3-compressed.arw; cmd_corpus (xtask main.rs:912-924) only fetches it on an explicit developer `cargo xtask corpus --download`, then hashes the file and compares it with the sha256 250784580ea52744... pinned on line 334.

verdicts.threatModel: The two advisories (GHSA-7w5x-hrqm-74c2 high, GHSA-r4xh-jqrq-34v2 moderate) are CPU-exhaustion DoS in smol-toml 1.7.0 parse() on malformed or adversarial TOML. An attacker must supply TOML text that reaches smol-toml's parse(); the only attacker capability that could do so here is write access to the repository's own manifests.
verdicts.reachability: smol-toml 1.7.0 enters only as a devDependency of @rightkit/release 0.2.124 (package.json:40 devDependencies; pnpm-lock.yaml:519-521; scanner path '.>@rightkit/release>smol-toml', dev:true). Its sole importer, @rightkit/release/ownership.mjs:4, calls parseToml only on Cargo.toml files of the scanned checkout (ownership.mjs:231,242) during maintainer-run release/ownership tooling. No product code imports it: the Tauri web frontend (apps/lightcraft-desktop/web) references neither smol-toml nor @rightkit/release, and the Rust product does not use npm packages. No network or end-user input reaches the parser.
verdicts.impact: None across a trust boundary. The parsed input is first-party Cargo.toml in the checkout; anyone able to modify it can already execute arbitrary code during the same build via build.rs or Cargo dependencies, so a parser hang grants no new capability. Worst case is a hung local release-tooling process, self-inflicted by whoever wrote the manifest; shipped binaries are unaffected. Scanner severity 'critical' also overstates the advisories (1 high, 1 moderate, 0 critical per scanner metadata).
verdicts.rationale: Vulnerable version is genuinely installed (dependency hygiene: bump @rightkit/release or smol-toml to >=1.9.0), but there is no attacker-controlled source, no trust boundary crossed, and no runtime/product reachability, so the candidate is not a security vulnerability.
verdicts.devilsAdvocate: Could a malicious contributor PR add a crafted Cargo.toml to hang CI? Anyone submitting a PR can already add an infinite loop in build.rs or a test, which CI executes anyway; CI job timeouts bound both. A third-party crate's Cargo.toml is not scanned (only checkout manifests selected from the repo), so supply-chain input does not reach parse().

verdicts.threatModel: Build-time supply chain only. The attacker must control the upstream publisher or its hosting: the AppImage/appimagetool GitHub `continuous` release asset (packaging/linux/package.sh:113) or the nuget.org package Microsoft.Trusted.Signing.Client (packaging/windows/sign.ps1:77). Transport is HTTPS (curl -fsSL to github.com; Invoke-WebRequest to https://www.nuget.org), so a network-position attacker cannot substitute content; no Ember user, file, or runtime input reaches either URL.
verdicts.reachability: Both downloads run only in release packaging. package.sh fetches appimagetool when neither APPIMAGETOOL nor an appimagetool on PATH exists and the cached copy is absent (lines 109-116); release.yml:223 runs it on ubuntu-22.04 runners that do not preinstall appimagetool, so it executes on every Linux release. sign.ps1 downloads the NuGet package only on the Azure Trusted Signing branch (lines 72-89), reached from package.ps1 in release.yml:158-171 when the AZURE_* secrets are set and WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE is not. Neither URL pins a version or digest: `continuous` is a mutable tag and the NuGet URL omits a version, resolving to latest.
verdicts.impact: No end-user attack surface. If upstream were compromised, the downloaded tool would execute in the release job: the appimagetool binary builds and embeds the runtime into the shipped AppImage (tampered release artifact), and the Azure dlib is loaded by signtool with AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET in the environment (credential exposure, signing of attacker content). Severity is bounded by needing a publisher-level compromise; the gap is missing pinning/hash verification, not an exploitable flaw reachable by an external attacker today. Missing pinning also makes release builds non-reproducible.
verdicts.rationale: Both cluster members are real unpinned, unhashed fetches of executable build tooling (package.sh:113 mutable `continuous` asset; sign.ps1:77 unversioned NuGet package), confirmed reachable from release.yml. Devil's advocate: HTTPS to first-party hosts, GitHub-hosted ephemeral runners, and the post-sign `signtool verify /pa` (sign.ps1:91) remove MITM and detect unsigned output, but do not detect a malicious upstream tool. No attacker-controlled source exists short of upstream compromise, so this is a supply-chain hardening gap (pin appimagetool to a tagged release with sha256; pin the NuGet package version and verify its hash), not a TRUE_POSITIVE.
